_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 6 specification: one article, six gaps, SEVEN sentences A–G, one of them extra. Each removed sentence hooks backwards by reference (she, those years, her plans, these new customers, this generosity, they) and forwards to the next sentence (a queue, the canteen, her reply, some of them, the loss, the notes on the board). The extra sentence (E) tempts gap 5, which is about low prices, but 'never once made a profit' contradicts the last paragraph, and it gives 'the loss' nothing specific to refer to. Used by the Part 6 practice page.
title: Bread for the night shift
subtitle: A former hospital porter opened a bakery that closes just as everyone else's opens. Her customers have never been happier to be awake at four in the morning.
text: At ten minutes to midnight, the narrow street behind Hallam General Hospital is dark and silent, except for one lit window. Inside, under a single warm lamp, Maggie Doyle is taking the first trays of cinnamon rolls out of the oven. {1} By half past twelve, a queue of nurses, cleaners and taxi drivers stretches past the launderette next door.

Night Loaf, as the bakery is called, opens at midnight and closes at six in the morning, just as most bakers are lighting their ovens. The idea came from Maggie's own experience. For nine years she worked nights as a hospital porter, pushing trolleys along empty corridors while the rest of the city slept. {2} The canteen closed at eight, the vending machines offered nothing but crisps and chocolate, and the only hot food for miles came from a petrol station.

'You'd finish a twelve-hour shift and the best thing on offer was a cold sausage roll in plastic,' she says. 'I used to dream about fresh bread.' When a bad back finally made portering impossible, she took a baking course and spent her savings on a tiny shop that had stood empty for two years. {3} Her reply was that she had no interest in sensible people, only tired ones.

Her first customers were former colleagues from the hospital, who came in on their breaks and then told everyone they knew. Within a month, word had spread to the cleaners who work in the city's office blocks overnight, and to the drivers who wait at the taxi rank by the station. {4} Some of them now have regular orders, which Maggie leaves ready in paper bags with their names on before they arrive.

The menu is short and rarely changes. There are rolls, soup in winter, a thick bacon sandwich and a lemon cake that one ambulance driver describes as 'the only reason I'm still in this job'. Prices are low, and anyone in a uniform gets their tea for free. {5} Maggie accepts the loss happily, although she admits that her accountant does not.

What customers value most, however, is not the food. Night workers often feel invisible, Maggie explains: they keep hospitals, offices and streets running, yet people mostly notice them only when something goes wrong. {6} On the wall by the counter is a board covered in notes from customers, thanking her for the hot chocolate, the conversation and, in one case, advice about a broken engagement.

Two years on, Night Loaf has made a small profit every month since its first winter, and Maggie has taken on a second baker, a former taxi driver called Dev. She still has no plans to open during the day. 'Daytime people have plenty of choice,' she says. 'Besides, I'd have to learn to sleep at night again, and I'm not sure I could.'
sentences: At Night Loaf, by contrast, someone is always pleased to see them, and they clearly appreciate it.
She has just ten minutes before she unlocks the door, and she knows exactly who will be waiting.
This generosity alone costs the bakery more than a hundred pounds a week.
When friends heard about her plans for it, they warned her that sensible people would be asleep at three in the morning.
Even with such low prices, she says, the bakery has never once made a profit.
What she remembers most about those years, though, is how hard it was to find anything decent to eat.
Many of these new customers come back every single night, and some come twice.
why: 'She' is Maggie, and ten minutes fits 'ten minutes to midnight'; 'who will be waiting' leads to the queue that forms by half past twelve.
'Those years' are her nine years as a night porter; the difficulty of finding food is explained by the closed canteen and the vending machines.
'It' is the tiny shop; the friends' warning about 'sensible people' is answered by 'Her reply… no interest in sensible people, only tired ones'.
'These new customers' are the cleaners and taxi drivers; coming back every night explains why 'some of them now have regular orders'.

'This generosity' is the free tea for anyone in uniform, and its cost is 'the loss' Maggie accepts. E is tempting after the low prices, but 'never once made a profit' contradicts the final paragraph, where the bakery has made a profit every month since its first winter.
'By contrast' sets the bakery against a world where night workers feel invisible; their appreciation leads to the board of thank-you notes.
